claim: Eukaryotes generally display a circadian rhythm as an adaptation to the reoccurring day/night cycle.
source: Eukaryotes generally display a circadian rhythm as an adaption to the reoccurring day/night cycle.
evidence: This is a general statement about eukaryotes supported by established scientific knowledge.

claim: Visual physiology is directly affected by changing light conditions.
source: This is particularly true for visual physiology that is directly affected by changing light conditions.
evidence: This statement is supported by established scientific understanding of visual systems.

claim: Transcript levels of most analyzed genes show a robust circadian rhythm-dependent regulation in zebrafish and mice.
source: Transcript as well as protein levels of most analyzed genes show a robust circadian rhythm-dependent regulation, which correlates with changes in photoresponse kinetics.
evidence: This claim is supported by qRT-PCR data presented in the manuscript showing oscillating transcript levels.

claim: Protein levels of most analyzed genes show a robust circadian rhythm-dependent regulation in zebrafish and mice.
source: Transcript as well as protein levels of most analyzed genes show a robust circadian rhythm-dependent regulation, which correlates with changes in photoresponse kinetics.
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data showing oscillating protein levels.

claim: Circadian rhythm-dependent regulation of gene expression correlates with changes in photoresponse kinetics.
source: Transcript as well as protein levels of most analyzed genes show a robust circadian rhythm-dependent regulation, which correlates with changes in photoresponse kinetics.
evidence: This claim is supported by ERG data showing changes in photoresponse recovery at different times of day.

claim: Photoresponse recovery in zebrafish is delayed in the evening.
source: Electroretinography demonstrates that photoresponse recovery in zebrafish is delayed in the evening and accelerated in the morning.
evidence: This claim is directly supported by ERG measurements presented in the manuscript.

claim: Photoresponse recovery in zebrafish is accelerated in the morning.
source: Electroretinography demonstrates that photoresponse recovery in zebrafish is delayed in the evening and accelerated in the morning.
evidence: This claim is directly supported by ERG measurements presented in the manuscript.

claim: Functional rhythmicity persists in continuous darkness.
source: Functional rhythmicity persists in continuous darkness, and it is reversed by an inverted light cycle and disrupted by constant light.
evidence: This claim is supported by ERG data from larvae kept in continuous darkness showing maintained circadian differences.

claim: Functional rhythmicity is reversed by an inverted light cycle.
source: Functional rhythmicity persists in continuous darkness, and it is reversed by an inverted light cycle and disrupted by constant light.
evidence: This claim is supported by ERG data from larvae raised in reversed light cycle conditions.

claim: Functional rhythmicity is disrupted by constant light.
source: Functional rhythmicity persists in continuous darkness, and it is reversed by an inverted light cycle and disrupted by constant light.
evidence: This claim is supported by ERG data from larvae kept under constant light showing loss of circadian differences.

claim: Orthologous gene transcripts from diurnal zebrafish and nocturnal mice are often expressed in an anti-phasic daily rhythm.
source: This is in line with our finding that orthologous gene transcripts from diurnal zebrafish and nocturnal mice are often expressed in an anti-phasic daily rhythm.
evidence: This claim is supported by qRT-PCR data comparing zebrafish and mouse gene expression patterns.

claim: The central pacemaker of circadian rhythms resides in the suprachiasmatic nucleus in mammals.
source: It has long been recognized that the central pacemaker of circadian rhythms resides in dedicated brain regions, either the suprachiasmatic nucleus in mammals or the pineal gland in non-mammalian vertebrates.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field of circadian biology.

claim: The central pacemaker of circadian rhythms resides in the pineal gland in non-mammalian vertebrates.
source: It has long been recognized that the central pacemaker of circadian rhythms resides in dedicated brain regions, either the suprachiasmatic nucleus in mammals or the pineal gland in non-mammalian vertebrates.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field of circadian biology.

claim: The circadian rhythm is entrained by external stimuli such as light that directly act on the core circadian transcriptional feedback loop.
source: The rhythm is entrained by external stimuli (eg, light) that directly act on the core circadian transcriptional feedback loop.
evidence: This is established knowledge about circadian rhythm entrainment.

claim: Autonomous circadian clocks exist in brain regions other than the central pacemaker and in peripheral tissues.
source: Multiple studies have shown that autonomous circadian clocks also exist in other brain regions and in peripheral tissues (Frøland Steindal and Whitmore, 2019; Idda et al., 2012; Vatine et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The retina generates its own circadian rhythm.
source: This is particularly true for the retina, which generates its own circadian rhythm (Gladys, 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Zebrafish show a higher response threshold in the morning as a circadian adaptation.
source: In zebrafish, this rhythmicity is reflected in a number of circadian adaptations, such as a higher response threshold in the morning (Li and Dowling, 1998), photoreceptor retinomotor movement in constant darkness (Menger et al., 2005), and cone photoreceptor synaptic ribbon disassembly at night (Emran et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Li and Dowling, 1998.

claim: Zebrafish show photoreceptor retinomotor movement in constant darkness as a circadian adaptation.
source: In zebrafish, this rhythmicity is reflected in a number of circadian adaptations, such as a higher response threshold in the morning (Li and Dowling, 1998), photoreceptor retinomotor movement in constant darkness (Menger et al., 2005), and cone photoreceptor synaptic ribbon disassembly at night (Emran et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Menger et al., 2005.

claim: Zebrafish show cone photoreceptor synaptic ribbon disassembly at night as a circadian adaptation.
source: In zebrafish, this rhythmicity is reflected in a number of circadian adaptations, such as a higher response threshold in the morning (Li and Dowling, 1998), photoreceptor retinomotor movement in constant darkness (Menger et al., 2005), and cone photoreceptor synaptic ribbon disassembly at night (Emran et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Emran et al., 2010.

claim: Mice show stronger electrical retinal coupling during the night.
source: Such adaptations are also found in other animals such as mice, where stronger electrical retinal coupling during the night (Jin et al., 2015; Li et al., 2009; Ribelayga et al., 2008), as well as slower dark adaptation of rods during the day, was observed (Xue et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Jin et al., 2015; Li et al., 2009; Ribelayga et al., 2008.

claim: Mice show slower dark adaptation of rods during the day.
source: Such adaptations are also found in other animals such as mice, where stronger electrical retinal coupling during the night (Jin et al., 2015; Li et al., 2009; Ribelayga et al., 2008), as well as slower dark adaptation of rods during the day, was observed (Xue et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Xue et al., 2015.

claim: The molecular mechanisms underlying circadian-dependent retinal regulations are still largely unknown.
source: The molecular mechanisms underlying these circadian-dependent retinal regulations are still largely unknown.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: There are two different types of photoreceptors in the vertebrate retina: rods and cones.
source: In the vertebrate retina, there are two different types of photoreceptors, namely rods and cones (Burns and Baylor, 2001; Fu and Yau, 2007).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Rods function mainly during dim light conditions.
source: Rods function mainly during dim light conditions, whereas cones are characterized by lower sensitivity but faster response kinetics, being important for daylight and color vision.
evidence: This is established knowledge about photoreceptor function.

claim: Cones are characterized by lower sensitivity but faster response kinetics compared to rods.
source: Rods function mainly during dim light conditions, whereas cones are characterized by lower sensitivity but faster response kinetics, being important for daylight and color vision.
evidence: This is established knowledge about photoreceptor function.

claim: Cones are important for daylight and color vision.
source: Rods function mainly during dim light conditions, whereas cones are characterized by lower sensitivity but faster response kinetics, being important for daylight and color vision.
evidence: This is established knowledge about photoreceptor function.

claim: About 92% of larval zebrafish photoreceptors are cones.
source: About 92% of larval and 60% of adult photoreceptors in the zebrafish retina are cones (Allison et al., 2010; Fadool, 2003; Zimmermann et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: About 60% of adult zebrafish photoreceptors are cones.
source: About 92% of larval and 60% of adult photoreceptors in the zebrafish retina are cones (Allison et al., 2010; Fadool, 2003; Zimmermann et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Rods and cones generally use the same visual transduction cascade components.
source: Although rods and cones generally use the same visual transduction cascade components, the individual reactions are typically mediated by photoreceptor type-specific proteins.
evidence: This is established knowledge about photoreceptor biochemistry.

claim: Individual reactions in the visual transduction cascade are typically mediated by photoreceptor type-specific proteins.
source: Although rods and cones generally use the same visual transduction cascade components, the individual reactions are typically mediated by photoreceptor type-specific proteins.
evidence: This is established knowledge about photoreceptor biochemistry.

claim: Visual transduction commences by an opsin chromophore-mediated absorption of photons.
source: Visual transduction commences by an opsin chromophore-mediated absorption of photons, which triggers the activation of a second messenger cascade including the trimeric G-protein transducin.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the visual transduction cascade.

claim: Photon absorption triggers the activation of a second messenger cascade including the trimeric G-protein transducin.
source: Visual transduction commences by an opsin chromophore-mediated absorption of photons, which triggers the activation of a second messenger cascade including the trimeric G-protein transducin.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the visual transduction cascade.

claim: Activated transducin stimulates the effector enzyme phosphodiesterase (PDE).
source: Activated transducin stimulates the effector enzyme phosphodiesterase (PDE), which leads to a reduction in intracellular cyclic guanosine monophosphate (cGMP) levels, subsequently leading to the closure of cyclic nucleotide -gated (CNG) cation channels, resulting in a membrane potential change (Fain et al., 2001; Lamb and Pugh, 2006).
evidence: This is established knowledge about the visual transduction cascade supported by citations.

claim: PDE activation leads to a reduction in intracellular cGMP levels.
source: Activated transducin stimulates the effector enzyme phosphodiesterase (PDE), which leads to a reduction in intracellular cyclic guanosine monophosphate (cGMP) levels, subsequently leading to the closure of cyclic nucleotide -gated (CNG) cation channels, resulting in a membrane potential change (Fain et al., 2001; Lamb and Pugh, 2006).
evidence: This is established knowledge about the visual transduction cascade supported by citations.

claim: Reduction in intracellular cGMP levels leads to the closure of cyclic nucleotide-gated (CNG) cation channels.
source: Activated transducin stimulates the effector enzyme phosphodiesterase (PDE), which leads to a reduction in intracellular cyclic guanosine monophosphate (cGMP) levels, subsequently leading to the closure of cyclic nucleotide -gated (CNG) cation channels, resulting in a membrane potential change (Fain et al., 2001; Lamb and Pugh, 2006).
evidence: This is established knowledge about the visual transduction cascade supported by citations.

claim: Closure of CNG cation channels results in a membrane potential change.
source: Activated transducin stimulates the effector enzyme phosphodiesterase (PDE), which leads to a reduction in intracellular cyclic guanosine monophosphate (cGMP) levels, subsequently leading to the closure of cyclic nucleotide -gated (CNG) cation channels, resulting in a membrane potential change (Fain et al., 2001; Lamb and Pugh, 2006).
evidence: This is established knowledge about the visual transduction cascade supported by citations.

claim: High-temporal resolution requires a tightly regulated termination of visual transduction.
source: High-temporal resolution requires a tightly regulated termination of visual transduction (Chen et al., 2012; Matthews and Sampath, 2010; Zang and Matthews, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Termination of visual transduction depends on the highly effective quenching of both the activated visual pigment (R*) and the PDE-transducin complex (PDE*).
source: This depends on the highly effective quenching of both the activated visual pigment (R*) and the PDE-transducin complex (PDE*).
evidence: This is established knowledge about visual transduction termination.

claim: R* is phosphorylated by a G-protein receptor kinase (GRK) before being completely deactivated by binding to arrestin.
source: R* is phosphorylated by a G-protein receptor kinase (GRK) before being completely deactivated by binding to arrestin.
evidence: This is established knowledge about visual pigment deactivation.

claim: GRK activity is controlled by recoverin (RCV) in a Ca2+-dependent manner.
source: While GRK activity itself is controlled by recoverin (RCV) in a Ca2+-dependent manner (Zang and Neuhauss, 2018), the quenching of PDE* depends on the GTPase activity of its γ-subunit that is regulated by activator protein RGS9 (Regulator of G-protein Signaling 9) (Krispel et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Zang and Neuhauss, 2018.

claim: The quenching of PDE* depends on the GTPase activity of its γ-subunit that is regulated by activator protein RGS9.
source: While GRK activity itself is controlled by recoverin (RCV) in a Ca2+-dependent manner (Zang and Neuhauss, 2018), the quenching of PDE* depends on the GTPase activity of its γ-subunit that is regulated by activator protein RGS9 (Regulator of G-protein Signaling 9) (Krispel et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Krispel et al., 2006.

claim: Expression levels of important regulators of cone visual transduction decay are modulated by the circadian clock.
source: We now show that the expression levels of these important regulators of cone visual transduction decay are modulated by the circadian clock.
evidence: This claim is supported by qRT-PCR data showing oscillating expression levels.

claim: Periodic fluctuations in gene expression are reflected in oscillating protein levels.
source: Moreover, these periodic fluctuations are reflected in oscillating protein levels that correlate with the rhythmicity in visual physiology and behavior observed in zebrafish.
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data showing oscillating protein levels.

claim: Oscillating protein levels correlate with the rhythmicity in visual physiology and behavior observed in zebrafish.
source: Moreover, these periodic fluctuations are reflected in oscillating protein levels that correlate with the rhythmicity in visual physiology and behavior observed in zebrafish.
evidence: This claim is supported by ERG and behavioral data showing circadian changes in visual function.

claim: Expression of mouse orthologs of the investigated regulatory genes is modulated by the circadian clock.
source: Interestingly, we have found that the expression of a selection of mouse orthologs of the investigated regulatory genes is also modulated by the circadian clock.
evidence: This claim is supported by qRT-PCR data from mouse retinas.

claim: The periodicity of mouse ortholog expression was opposite to that of zebrafish, fitting the nocturnal lifestyle of mice.
source: However, the periodicity was opposite to that of zebrafish, fitting the nocturnal lifestyle of mice.
evidence: This claim is supported by comparative qRT-PCR data from zebrafish and mice.

claim: Apart from rcv2a, expression levels of recoverins, G-protein receptor kinases, arrestins, and rgs9a were clearly oscillating in zebrafish.
source: Apart from rcv2a, which seems to have no or weak fluctuating transcript levels in larvae (Figure 1G), expression levels of the other recoverins (rcv1a, rcv1b, which is absent from larval retina, and rcv2b), G-protein receptor kinases (grk7a and grk7b), arrestins (arr3a and arr3b), and regulator of G-protein signaling 9 (rgs9a) were clearly oscillating (statistical information in Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 1.

claim: rcv2a has no or weak fluctuating transcript levels in zebrafish larvae.
source: Apart from rcv2a, which seems to have no or weak fluctuating transcript levels in larvae (Figure 1G), expression levels of the other recoverins (rcv1a, rcv1b, which is absent from larval retina, and rcv2b), G-protein receptor kinases (grk7a and grk7b), arrestins (arr3a and arr3b), and regulator of G-protein signaling 9 (rgs9a) were clearly oscillating (statistical information in Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: rcv1b is absent from larval zebrafish retina.
source: Apart from rcv2a, which seems to have no or weak fluctuating transcript levels in larvae (Figure 1G), expression levels of the other recoverins (rcv1a, rcv1b, which is absent from larval retina, and rcv2b), G-protein receptor kinases (grk7a and grk7b), arrestins (arr3a and arr3b), and regulator of G-protein signaling 9 (rgs9a) were clearly oscillating (statistical information in Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by qRT-PCR data showing no rcv1b expression in larvae.

claim: In many cases, transcripts were most abundant at ZT1 or ZT4 in zebrafish.
source: In many cases, transcripts were most abundant at ZT1 or ZT4 (grk7a, grk7b, rcv2b, arr3a, and arr3b), subsequently declined throughout the day, and recovered during the night.
evidence: This claim is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 1.

claim: Transcripts of grk7a, grk7b, rcv2b, arr3a, and arr3b declined throughout the day and recovered during the night in zebrafish.
source: In many cases, transcripts were most abundant at ZT1 or ZT4 (grk7a, grk7b, rcv2b, arr3a, and arr3b), subsequently declined throughout the day, and recovered during the night.
evidence: This claim is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 1.

claim: In adult zebrafish eyes, grk7a expression levels decreased by around 98% from the peak to the lowest expression level.
source: For instance, in adult zebrafish eyes, grk7a expression levels decreased by around 98% from the peak to the lowest expression level (Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: In adult zebrafish, rgs9a transcripts reached the highest level at ZT22, with the value very close to ZT1.
source: In the case of adult rgs9a, transcripts reached the highest level at ZT22, with the value very close to ZT1.
evidence: This claim is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 1I.

claim: In situ hybridization (ISH) analysis validated the qRT-PCR results.
source: In situ hybridization (ISH) analysis using digoxigenin-labeled RNA probes validated our qRT-PCR results (Figure 1—figure supplement 2 and Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by ISH data shown in the figure supplements.

claim: rcv1a and rcv2a displayed different expression profiles in larval and adult zebrafish eyes.
source: Interestingly, two genes, namely rcv1a and rcv2a, displayed different expression profiles in larval and adult eyes (Figure 1E&G).
evidence: This claim is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 1E and 1G.

claim: Larval rcv1a mRNA transcript levels peaked around ZT19.
source: While larval rcv1a mRNA transcript levels peaked around ZT19, larval rcv2a transcript expression was weak/non-cyclic.
evidence: This claim is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Larval rcv2a transcript expression was weak/non-cyclic.
source: While larval rcv1a mRNA transcript levels peaked around ZT19, larval rcv2a transcript expression was weak/non-cyclic.
evidence: This claim is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: In adult zebrafish retinas, rcv1a and rcv2a transcripts were highest at ZT7.
source: However, this is in contrast to adult retinas where rcv1a and rcv2a transcripts were highest at ZT7 (Figure 1G).
evidence: This claim is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: An anti-phasic expression profile between larval and adult stages can be observed for rod arrestins (arras).
source: An anti-phasic expression profile between larval and adult stages can also be observed for rod arrestins (arras) (Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4.

claim: Under normal LD and DD conditions, largely comparable results were obtained for gene expression.
source: Under normal LD, as well as DD conditions, we obtained largely comparable results (Figure 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by qRT-PCR data comparing LD and DD conditions shown in Figure 1.

claim: arr3a and arr3b showed a 3-hr phase shift between LD and DD conditions.
source: Exceptions were arr3a and arr3b, showing a 3-hr phase shift, and rcv1a, showing an almost anti-phase relationship (see 'Discussion' section).
evidence: This claim is supported by qRT-PCR data comparing LD and DD conditions shown in Figure 1.

claim: rcv1a showed an almost anti-phase relationship between LD and DD conditions.
source: Exceptions were arr3a and arr3b, showing a 3-hr phase shift, and rcv1a, showing an almost anti-phase relationship (see 'Discussion' section).
evidence: This claim is supported by qRT-PCR data comparing LD and DD conditions shown in Figure 1.

claim: Expression of all five mouse regulators (Grk1, Recvrn, Rgs9, Arrb1, and Arrb3) fluctuated in a 24 hr period.
source: Expression of all five regulators fluctuated in a 24 hr period (Figure 2), being highest at the beginning of the dark period (ZT13) for the two arrestins (Figure 2A&B), or around midnight (ZT17) for Grk1, Rgs1, and Recvrn (Figure 2C–E).
evidence: This claim is supported by qRT-PCR data from mouse retinas shown in Figure 2.

claim: Mouse arrestins Arrb1 and Arrb3 were highest at the beginning of the dark period (ZT13).
source: Expression of all five regulators fluctuated in a 24 hr period (Figure 2), being highest at the beginning of the dark period (ZT13) for the two arrestins (Figure 2A&B), or around midnight (ZT17) for Grk1, Rgs1, and Recvrn (Figure 2C–E).
evidence: This claim is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 2A and 2B.

claim: Mouse Grk1, Rgs9, and Recvrn were highest around midnight (ZT17).
source: Expression of all five regulators fluctuated in a 24 hr period (Figure 2), being highest at the beginning of the dark period (ZT13) for the two arrestins (Figure 2A&B), or around midnight (ZT17) for Grk1, Rgs1, and Recvrn (Figure 2C–E).
evidence: This claim is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 2C-E.

claim: All mouse genes displayed minimal transcript levels early during the day.
source: All of them displayed minimal transcript levels early during the day.
evidence: This claim is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 2.

claim: The oscillation pattern of mouse genes shows a clear anti-phasic relationship with the cyclic fluctuation of the corresponding zebrafish transcripts.
source: This oscillation pattern shows a clear anti-phasic relationship with the cyclic fluctuation of the corresponding zebrafish transcripts.
evidence: This claim is supported by comparative analysis of qRT-PCR data from zebrafish and mice.

claim: The amplitude of gene fluctuation in adult zebrafish retina was generally larger than that in the mouse retina.
source: Curiously, the amplitude of gene fluctuation in adult zebrafish retina was generally larger than that in the mouse retina (Figures 1 and 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparative analysis of qRT-PCR data shown in Figures 1 and 2.

claim: mRNA half-life is typically in the range of minutes.
source: While mRNA half-life is typically in the range of minutes, protein turnover rates can range from minutes to days, explaining why fluctuation of mRNA levels is not always reflected in time-shifted oscillations at the protein level (Cunningham and Gonzalez-Fernandez, 2000; Stenkamp et al., 2005).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Protein turnover rates can range from minutes to days.
source: While mRNA half-life is typically in the range of minutes, protein turnover rates can range from minutes to days, explaining why fluctuation of mRNA levels is not always reflected in time-shifted oscillations at the protein level (Cunningham and Gonzalez-Fernandez, 2000; Stenkamp et al., 2005).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Fluctuation of mRNA levels is not always reflected in time-shifted oscillations at the protein level.
source: While mRNA half-life is typically in the range of minutes, protein turnover rates can range from minutes to days, explaining why fluctuation of mRNA levels is not always reflected in time-shifted oscillations at the protein level (Cunningham and Gonzalez-Fernandez, 2000; Stenkamp et al., 2005).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Regulatory proteins often have turnover rates of only a few hours.
source: However, as regulatory proteins often have turnover rates of only a few hours, we were examining whether RNA oscillations are mirrored by corresponding protein level fluctuations.
evidence: This is established knowledge about protein turnover.

claim: Quantitative western blot analysis indicated periodic changes in protein levels for both GRK7a and ARR3a.
source: Quantitative western blot analysis indicated periodic changes in protein levels for both proteins.
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Peak expression was shifted 6-12 hr between RNA and protein level for GRK7a and ARR3a.
source: Peak expression was shifted 6 - 12 hr between RNA and protein level (Figure 3A&B).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of qRT-PCR and Western blot data shown in Figure 3.

claim: ARR3a reached its highest and lowest levels at ZT7 and ZT22, respectively.
source: ARR3a reached its highest and lowest levels at ZT7 and ZT22, respectively, whereas GRK7a maintained relatively high levels throughout the day, having the lowest concentrations around midnight.
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: GRK7a maintained relatively high levels throughout the day, having the lowest concentrations around midnight.
source: ARR3a reached its highest and lowest levels at ZT7 and ZT22, respectively, whereas GRK7a maintained relatively high levels throughout the day, having the lowest concentrations around midnight.
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: mRNA circadian oscillations in the zebrafish retina are largely conserved at the protein level with a time shift.
source: Hence, mRNA circadian oscillations in the zebrafish retina are largely conserved at the protein level with a time shift.
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of qRT-PCR and Western blot data.

claim: Photoresponses at larval zebrafish stages are dominated by cone photoreceptors.
source: Photoresponses at larval zebrafish stages are dominated by cone photoreceptors (Bilotta et al., 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Bilotta et al., 2001.

claim: In the zebrafish ERG, the a-wave is largely masked by the larger b-wave.
source: In the electroretinogram (ERG), the a-wave directly represents photoreceptor responses. Since in the zebrafish ERG, it is largely masked by the larger b-wave, reflecting the depolarization of ON-bipolar cells, we used the b-wave amplitude as an indirect measure of the cone photoresponse (Figure 4A1).
evidence: This is established knowledge about zebrafish ERG.

claim: The ERG b-wave reflects the depolarization of ON-bipolar cells.
source: In the electroretinogram (ERG), the a-wave directly represents photoreceptor responses. Since in the zebrafish ERG, it is largely masked by the larger b-wave, reflecting the depolarization of ON-bipolar cells, we used the b-wave amplitude as an indirect measure of the cone photoresponse (Figure 4A1).
evidence: This is established knowledge about ERG components.

claim: The protein products of the genes analyzed affect photoresponse recovery in zebrafish.
source: The protein products of the genes analyzed in our study are known to affect photoresponse recovery in zebrafish (Renninger et al., 2011; Rinner et al., 2005; Zang et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Response recovery was significantly delayed in the evening in comparison to the morning.
source: Response recovery was significantly delayed in the evening in comparison to the morning (Figure 4A2).
evidence: This claim is supported by ERG data shown in Figure 4A2.

claim: The double-flash paradigm demonstrated that the a-wave response recovery in the evening was delayed.
source: Consistently, the double-flash paradigm demonstrated that the a-wave response recovery in the evening was delayed (Figure 4B2).
evidence: This claim is supported by ERG a-wave data shown in Figure 4B2.

claim: The a-wave was contributed by all cone subtypes according to the light spectrum.
source: According to the light spectrum (Figure 4—figure supplement 2), the a-wave was contributed by all cone subtypes.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the light spectrum data.

claim: In larvae kept in constant darkness, the decrease in response recovery at corresponding time points was comparable to LD conditions.
source: At corresponding time points, the decrease in response recovery was comparable (Figure 4C1&C2), verifying that the observed changes are regulated by an intrinsic circadian clock.
evidence: This claim is supported by ERG data from DD larvae shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The observed changes in response recovery are regulated by an intrinsic circadian clock.
source: At corresponding time points, the decrease in response recovery was comparable (Figure 4C1&C2), verifying that the observed changes are regulated by an intrinsic circadian clock.
evidence: This claim is supported by ERG data from DD larvae showing maintained circadian differences.

claim: The normalized power at each stimulus frequency was significantly weaker in the evening compared with the power in the morning.
source: In line with our hypothesis, we found that the normalized power at each stimulus frequency was significantly weaker in the evening compared with the power in the morning.
evidence: This claim is supported by flicker ERG data shown in Figure 5.

claim: The cone visual temporal resolution is under circadian control.
source: This clearly indicates that the cone visual temporal resolution is under circadian control.
evidence: This claim is inferred from flicker ERG data showing time-of-day differences.

claim: The flicker ERG was mainly contributed by double-cone responses because of the spectral content of the stimulus light.
source: Note here, the flicker ERG was mainly contributed by double-cone responses because of the spectral content of the stimulus light (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the light spectrum data.

claim: Under reversed light cycle (DL), gene expression levels stayed in the fish's time.
source: Under this condition, gene expression levels stayed in the fish's time.
evidence: This claim is supported by ISH data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: ISH for the genes of interest reflected stronger staining intensity in LD fish at 9 o'clock in the morning compared to DL fish at the same time.
source: ISH for the genes of interest (Figure 6A) reflected this, with a stronger staining intensity in LD fish at 9 o'clock in the morning compared to DL fish at the same time.
evidence: This claim is supported by ISH data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: When both LD and DL groups were recorded at 120 hr post fertilization, a prolonged response recovery time was obtained in the fish maintained in reversed light cycle.
source: Consequently, when both groups were recorded at 120 hr post fertilization, a prolonged response recovery time was obtained in the fish maintained in reversed light cycle, reflecting the situation in fish kept in the normal light and recorded in the evening (Figure 6D).
evidence: This claim is supported by ERG data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Continuous light exposure has been shown to disrupt the intrinsic circadian rhythm.
source: While the intrinsic circadian clock is maintained in the absence of light, continuous light exposure has been shown to disrupt this intrinsic rhythm (Laranjeiro and Whitmore, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Laranjeiro and Whitmore, 2014.

claim: The gene expression differences between morning and evening detected under LD conditions were completely lost in LL larvae.
source: Strikingly, the gene expression differences between morning and evening detected under LD conditions were completely lost in LL larvae (Figure 6B&C).
evidence: This claim is supported by ISH and qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 6B and 6C.

claim: Under constant light, there was no delay of photoresponse recovery in the evening.
source: This was also reflected on a functional level with no delay of photoresponse recovery in the evening, as measured by ERG.
evidence: This claim is supported by ERG data from LL larvae shown in Figure 6E.

claim: Changes in the light cycle are reflected in changes of transcript levels of phototransduction regulators that subsequently lead to altered visual performance at different times during the day.
source: Taken together, these results demonstrate that changes in the light cycle are reflected in changes of transcript levels of phototransduction regulators that subsequently lead to altered visual performance at different times during the day.
evidence: This claim is supported by the combined data from gene expression and ERG experiments under different light conditions.

claim: The decay of photoresponse to different light intensities in the model was largely prolonged in the evening.
source: As predicted by our experimental results, the decay of photoresponse to different light intensities in the model was largely prolonged in the evening (Figure 7A–E).
evidence: This claim is supported by computational modeling results shown in Figure 7.

claim: Circadian gene regulation helps the organism to optimally adapt to its preferential lifestyle and/or environment.
